name: West Route

waypoints.name: Arrow Creek switchback (Illabot Creek Road / FR-16)
waypoints.note: Not Kindy Creek Road, the trailhead for neighboring Snowking Mountain. The trailhead here is FR-16 (Illabot Creek Road) at the Arrow Creek switchback. Boot/fisherman's path leaves the road ~20 yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing.
waypoints.directions: Drive Highway 530 to Illabot Creek Road (FR-16) and follow it to the Arrow Creek switchback at about 2,220 ft. This is the trailhead, but not a formal one, so park on the road at the switchback and expect no lot and nothing signed. The boot path leaves the road roughly 20 yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south bank of Illabot Creek upstream.

waypoints.name: Cliff/gully route-finding crux
waypoints.note: Band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000-4,300 ft — the route-finding crux of the approach; intermittent cairns/flagging at best.
waypoints.directions: Take the unsigned fisherman's path from the road and follow it upstream along the south side of Illabot Creek through old growth for about a mile, then turn uphill near the first major side creek, which can be a wet ford early in the season. Angle southeast and uphill around a belt of slide alder to the band of cliffs and gullies at about 4,000 to 4,300 ft; cairns and flagging are sparse here and it is easy to commit to the wrong gully.

waypoints.name: Base of west face ramp
waypoints.note: Open west-facing slopes below/west of Pt. 4593', traverse east to the base of Chaval's broad west face and the diagonal ascent ramp.

approach: The hike-in starts where FR-16 (Illabot Creek Road) reaches the Arrow Creek switchback (~2,220 ft) — this is the trailhead, not a formal one. A boot/fisherman's path leaves the road roughly 20 yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south (right) bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it's reasonably distinct and has occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned, so expect some searching. Follow it about a mile, then look for a crossing to the north side of the drainage near a significant side-creek confluence — this can be an easy boulder-hop by late summer or a genuine wet ford in early season, so check flow before committing (it's the approach's main creek-ford hazard). Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder and brush (the worst brush of the day) trending southeast, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000–4,300 ft — this is the route-finding crux of the approach: intermittent cairns/flagging at best, and it's easy to end up in the wrong gully. A GPS track of a prior ascent (or careful use of a described waypoint like Point 4593') is genuinely useful here. The last dependable water is around 4,000 ft, right before the terrain opens up; above that, water is snow-patch dependent into midsummer. From there the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes below/west of Pt. 4593', and you traverse and climb east to reach the base of Chaval's broad west face, where the ascent line's obvious left-to-right diagonal ramp begins. Figure roughly 2,000–2,500 ft of gain and 2-3 miles from the Arrow Creek trailhead to the base of the ramp, with parties reporting 4-5 hours car-to-ramp; the gullies just below the west face are avalanche terrain and should not be crossed in unstable early-season snow, and steep sidehilling with real exposure starts once you're above treeline.

approach_variants.name: Illabot Creek Road, Arrow Creek switchback and the west slopes
approach_variants.notes: The trailhead is not a formal one — it is the point where the Illabot Creek Road reaches the Arrow Creek switchback, and you park on the road. A boot and fisherman's path leaves the road about twenty yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it is reasonably distinct with occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned. Follow it about a mile, then look for a crossing to the north side of the drainage near a significant side-creek confluence — an easy boulder hop by late summer, a genuine wet ford in early season, so check the flow before committing. Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder, which is the worst brush of the day, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000 to 4,300 ft. That band is the route-finding crux of the walk-in: intermittent cairns and flagging at best, and it is easy to end up in the wrong gully. Last dependable water is around 4,000 ft. Above, the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes and traverses and climbs east toward the summit block.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September. The road and the approach gullies typically do not clear of snow until July, and the peak sees almost no traffic outside that narrow window.
hazards: a pathless, committing approach through steep brushy old growth with stream crossings and sustained sidehilling
the cliff-and-gully band at 4,000 to 4,300 ft, where it is easy to commit to the wrong gully in either direction
snow-filled entrance gullies below the west face that can sluff or slide in warm or unstable conditions
exposed, moss- and heather-covered steps on the summit block ramp, worse descending than ascending
weak and unreliable water above 4,000 ft
frequent afternoon thunderstorms in the approach basins
approach_variants.baseFinding: You must cross to the north side of the ridge before the ramp exists. From the open west slopes, climb northeast across the basin and up a steep gully to a pass in the ridge at about 5,920 ft, then cross over to the north side of that ridge and traverse east until the west face of the summit block is in front of you. The line up that face is one large, obvious ramp, and its direction is the test: it climbs the face diagonally from left to right to reach the summit ridge, where you turn left and scramble to the top. If the ramp you are looking at runs right to left, or if you are still on the south side of the ridge, you have not reached the correct face. If you can see no single dominant ramp at all — just broken ground and heather steps — you are still short of the summit block and should keep traversing east. The rock on the ramp carries heather and moss rather than clean stone, so treat it as insecure, and note that the same ground is considerably harder facing outward on the way down.

descent_text: Descent is a reversal of the ascent line, not a walk-off in a different direction: downclimb the same diagonal west-face ramp back down to roughly 4,000-4,300 ft, re-enter the gully/cliff-band system, and pick back down through the brush and slide-alder benches to regain Illabot Creek, re-crossing to the south bank near the same spot used on the way up before following the fisherman's path back to the Arrow Creek trailhead. There is no cairned or maintained route for most of this, so route-finding is the primary descent hazard — it's easy to drop into the wrong gully in the cliff band, and carrying a GPS breadcrumb of your ascent (or flagging key turns) is standard practice. The heather- and moss-covered rock on the ramp is more hazardous descending than climbing since holds face the wrong way and the exposure reads more obviously on the way down; a short, steep, exposed Class 3 section near the top of the ramp is where a party might reasonably choose to place a hand line, though this is discretionary, not standard practice. This is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed anchors, no bolted rappel stations, and no established rappels — crampons are occasionally useful on lingering snow patches, but a rope is not standard.
